title: A grid is a graph
sub: Flood Fill and Number of Islands: a cell is a vertex, a neighbor is an edge, recursion versus an explicit stack
cards/0/title: The problem and the graph you don't see
cards/0/body:
Flood Fill (LeetCode #733). An image is an m×n grid image, with m and n up to 50. You are given a start (sr, sc) and a color. Repaint the start pixel and every pixel of its color that can be reached from it by steps up, down, left and right. It is the paint bucket from any image editor.

Graph traversal signals: “can be reached”, “connected”, “region”, “adjacent cells”. No graph is drawn here, but there is one: a cell is a vertex, sharing a side is an edge. There are m·n vertices, each with at most four neighbors, so at most 2·m·n edges. No adjacency lists are needed: offsets give the neighbors, as in u3.l5.

Depth-first search (DFS): paint the cell and call yourself on its four neighbors. A call that steps off the edge or lands on another color returns at once. Repainting doubles as the “visited” mark: a painted cell no longer has the original color, so nobody enters it twice. Each cell is painted once and checked from at most four neighbors — O(m·n) time.
cards/1/q: The start != color check was removed from FloodFill, so Fill is always called. What happens on image = [[1, 1]], sr = 0, sc = 0, color = 1?
cards/1/options/0: Fill paints (0, 0) from 1 to 1, goes to (0, 1), from there back to (0, 0) — on and on until the stack overflows
cards/1/options/1: The same image comes back: repainting 1 as 1 does nothing
cards/1/options/2: Fill repaints both cells once each and returns
cards/1/options/3: The compiler warns that from and to may be equal
cards/1/explain: The “visited” mark here is the change of color. If from == to, a painted cell keeps the color from, and the img[r][c] != from check doesn't stop it: (0, 0) → (0, 1) → (0, 0) → … The depth grows until the stack runs out, and StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET — the process terminates (u1.l3). A separate visited array would survive even this, but in this problem it is simpler to return right away.
cards/1/wrong/1: A single repaint would do nothing, but recursive calls follow it. They can't tell the cell was visited: its color didn't change.
cards/1/wrong/2: Only the mark guarantees “once each”. When the color doesn't change there is no mark, and the cells are visited again and again.
cards/1/wrong/3: The code is valid as far as the language goes: the compiler doesn't check whether two int parameters are equal. The bug shows up only at run time.
cards/2/title: Number of Islands: how many times the traversal started
cards/2/body:
Number of Islands (LeetCode #200). An m×n grid, up to 300×300, of the characters '1' (land) and '0' (water). An island is land connected through sides; diagonal cells are not neighbors. Count the islands.

Idea. An outer loop visits every cell. When it meets land that no traversal has touched yet, that is a new island: count++, and the DFS Sink “sinks” the whole island by writing '0', so the loop doesn't count its cells again. The answer is the number of DFS launches, that is, the number of connected components of the land graph.

Invariant: whenever the outer loop stands on a cell, every island it has already counted is fully sunk. So any '1' under the loop belongs to a new island.

Cost. The loop walks m·n cells, Sink enters each land cell once — O(m·n) time. The input gets destroyed along the way; if that's not allowed, keep a bool[,] visited. Whether the grid may be modified is a question for the interviewer.
cards/3/explain: The counter grows on every Sink launch — one launch sinks one island. The grid has g.Length rows and g[0].Length columns: on a non-square map, swapped bounds index out of the array. Compare with the character '1', not the number 1: a char in C# is a number, and '1' equals 49. The mark is writing '0'; after it the loop no longer sees the cell. The four calls go down, up, right, left.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on a 5×6 map. Color is the island number; below is the stack of Sink calls. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next: keep track of who is running — the outer loop or the recursion.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Sink(1, 0) returns to Sink(0, 0), which goes right and sinks (0, 1)
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: The outer loop finds (0, 1): that is island #2
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Island #1 is done: it has two cells, (0, 0) and (1, 0)
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Sink(1, 0): water below, (0, 0) above is already sunk, water to the right, the edge to the left. What next?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: Sink(1, 0) has returned, but Sink(0, 0) isn't finished: it checked down (that's where it went) and up (the edge), and right is next — (0, 1), land of the same island. The outer loop regains control only once the whole island is sunk, so it will never see (0, 1) as new land.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Island #4 is sunk: (3, 5), (4, 5) and (4, 4). The outer loop continues row by row. What will it find?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: (4, 4) is land on the original map, but the DFS from (3, 5) reached it through (4, 5) and sank it. The loop finishes row 3, starts row 4 and immediately meets (4, 0) — untouched land: count = 5, and Sink will sink (4, 0) and (4, 1). That's the invariant at work: whatever is still '1' under the loop is a new island.
cards/5/title: Recursion depth: 50×50 is fine, 300×300 is not
cards/5/body:
The stack holds the current chain of DFS calls — from the cell where the traversal began to the cell it is handling now. On solid land Sink snakes: down to the edge, one step right, up to the edge, right again… No call returns until every cell is covered, and the depth equals the number of cells in the region. Small islands on a huge map are safe, though: the depth is bounded by the size of the island, not of the grid.

The numbers. In u10.l3 a recursive frame was estimated at 50–60 bytes; Fill and Sink take more parameters, and on x64 their frame comes out at 50–100 bytes, so a 1 MB stack holds on the order of 10⁴–2·10⁴ frames. Flood Fill at 50×50 is at most 2500 frames, 150–250 KB: safe. Number of Islands at 300×300 of solid land is 9·10⁴ frames, 5–9 MB: it doesn't fit in 1 MB. (On Linux the main thread usually gets 8 MB, which is why such a solution sometimes passes on a judge — don't count on it.) A 1000×1000 tile map is 10⁶ frames. A stack overflow cannot be caught (u1.l3), and a recursive fill launched from an editor tool can take the Unity Editor down along with the unsaved scene.

The cure from u1.l3 is an explicit stack on the heap. One detail: mark a cell when you push it, not when you pop it. Then each cell enters the stack once, and the stack never exceeds m·n. If you mark on pop, each of the four neighbors may push the same cell before its turn comes.
cards/6/q: The stack is 1 MB and a frame of the recursive traversal is 50–100 bytes. On which inputs is recursive DFS safe? Select all.
cards/6/options/0: Flood Fill #733: an image up to 50×50
cards/6/options/1: Number of Islands #200: 300×300, almost all land
cards/6/options/2: A 1000×1000 map whose islands have at most 100 cells each
cards/6/options/3: A 1000×1000 map with a one-cell-wide snake road half a million cells long
cards/6/explain: The depth equals the size of the region being filled. 50×50 is at most 2500 frames. Islands of 100 cells go no deeper than 100, however big the map is. On solid water Sink is never called at all. Almost solid land at 300×300 is up to 9·10⁴ frames, 5–9 MB; the snake is 5·10⁵: neither fits in a megabyte.
cards/7/title: BFS and DFS: one template, two structures
cards/7/body:
Replace Stack with Queue in the explicit traversal, and the same loop becomes breadth-first search, the BFS from u10.l1. Both work for filling and for counting islands, both are O(m·n): all that matters is that each cell is processed once. What differs is order and memory.

DFS follows one line as far as it goes and only then backs up: the fill crawls like a snake (you'll see it on the rig next). On a snake the explicit stack holds up to m·n cells.
BFS moves in waves: first every cell one step from the start, then two steps… Cells leave the queue in order of distance, so BFS also gives the shortest number of steps. The queue holds only the wave front: on an open map that is on the order of m + n cells (about 2000 from the center of 1000×1000), although on a tangled map the worst case is O(m·n) as well.

Rule: if you only need connectivity or the region itself, any traversal works — without recursion on a big grid. If you need “nearest” or “fewest steps”, only BFS: the path along which DFS reached a cell need not be the shortest.
cards/8/task: Step through the recursive fill from (1, 1): every connected 1 becomes a 2. The rig will ask twice what the code does next. Keep the call order in mind: down, up, right, left.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: (0, 2) is painted. Its neighbors: 0 below, the edge above, 0 to the right, (0, 1) to the left — already 2. Which cell will the code paint next?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: Fill(0, 2) returns empty-handed, and control comes back to Fill(0, 1): down, up and right are checked there, left remains — (0, 0). (1, 0) is a neighbor of the start itself: BFS would paint it in the very first wave, but DFS reaches it only from (0, 0). (1, 2) is 0, not the original color.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Find the next region of ones and repaint it
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: (2, 0) is painted. 0 below, already 2 above, 0 to the right, the edge to the left. What next?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: From (2, 0) you can reach (3, 1) only diagonally, and neighbors share a side. The ones at the bottom right are another region, and Flood Fill leaves it alone: there is no outer loop here, unlike in islands. The calls unwind back to the very first one; 6 cells are repainted, each once.
cards/9/q: On the map from the rig (5 islands) this code returns 13 — the number of land cells on it. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: g[r][c] is a char, and compared with the number 1 it turns into its code: '1' is 49, and 49 != 1 is always true. Sink returns immediately without sinking anything, and the outer loop counts every land cell as a separate island. The code compiles without a warning — it needs the character: g[r][c] != '1'.
cards/10/title: In a game: tile fill and connected regions
cards/10/body:
Filling tiles. Tilemap has a built-in FloodFill(position, tile). But for game logic — “which cells will the water flood”, “which area has the player captured” — your own traversal over an array is handier: Tilemap is slow for logic (u3.l5).

Region labels. The same outer loop as in islands, but instead of '0' the traversal writes the region number into int[] region. Now “can I get from A to B” is region[a] == region[b], O(1) without any pathfinding. That's how unreachable targets are rejected before A* runs; otherwise it would comb the entire region before giving up. Recompute the labels when the map changes: a door opened, a wall collapsed.

Caves. After a cellular automaton the map falls apart into regions. Labels find the small ones — they get filled in — and the large ones, which are later joined by corridors (choosing the corridors is lesson 5).

Variations. Island area (#695): the traversal returns the number of cells. Eight-connectivity: eight offsets, and islands touching at a corner merge into one. Don't destroy the input: bool[] visited. The queue here is a plain int[] of w·h cells: each cell enters it once, so two indices, head and tail, are enough, with no allocations on repeated calls.
cards/10/deep:
No allocations. The local function Push captures count, tail and the arrays. As long as it isn't converted to a delegate, the compiler puts the captured variables in a struct on the stack — there is no heap object. Array.Fill exists since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, that is, in Unity 2021.2 and later.

Jobs and Burst. The traversal itself is sequential, but it can move off the main thread: an IJob with NativeArray<int> instead of arrays, and Burst compiles the loop. Labeling can be parallelized by chunks: each chunk is labeled on its own, and labels that touch across chunk borders are merged with the disjoint-set structure from lesson 5 — the classic two-pass connected-component labeling.

Partial recomputation. Destroying a wall can only merge regions, so there is no need to relabel the whole map. Building a wall may cut a region in two — then relabel just that region.

Four or eight neighbors. If land counts as connected diagonally, water must be connected only through sides — otherwise two diagonals “cross”: land and water both pass through the same point. That's why image processing uses different connectivity for the background and for the objects.
cards/11/q: You are solving Number of Islands out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: neighbors through sides or diagonals too, may the grid be modified, what are the sizes
cards/11/items/1: Reduce to a graph: a cell is a vertex, a side neighbor is an edge, the answer is the number of land components
cards/11/items/2: Idea: an outer loop; on every untouched land cell count++, and a traversal sinks the whole island
cards/11/items/3: Code: mark a cell on entry; at 300×300 use an explicit stack instead of recursion
cards/11/items/4: Run it on a small map where two islands touch at a corner
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(m·n) time and O(m·n) memory in the worst case
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: all water, all land, a single row
cards/11/explain: Connectivity (4 or 8 neighbors) changes the answer, so it is clarified first. The reduction to a graph names the pattern; then the idea, the code with the depth caveat, an example with corners to check connectivity, and then the cost. “All land” is exactly the case where recursion crashes.
cards/12/q: Match the requirement to the technique.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: The traversal returns the cell count
cards/12/pairs/1/0: Islands touching at a corner are one
cards/12/pairs/2/0: The grid must not be modified
cards/12/pairs/3/1: An explicit stack or a queue
